evidence.finding: Mean logged-in staffing declined 26.7%, from 49 before the incident to 35.9 afterward, reaching 33 agents despite 49 remaining scheduled.
Mean productive staffing declined 25.6%, from 45.2 to 33.6 agents, with a low of 31 versus forecast requirements of 35–39 agents.
Scheduled staffing remained constant at 49 and no agents were in training, isolating the capacity loss to same-day availability rather than scheduling or training.
Mean service level fell 23.5 percentage points, from 90.3% before the incident to 66.9% afterward.
Mean ASA rose from 25.2 to 56.7 seconds, a 124.7% increase, while post-incident occupancy averaged 90.6% and reached 100%.
Offered calls increased 6.0% versus the pre-incident mean, adding moderate pressure but not constituting a demand spike.
All four queues experienced staffing reductions of approximately 24.7%–28.9% and material service-level declines, demonstrating a center-wide capacity problem rather than an isolated queue failure.
The only visible event was a center-wide workforce notice at 09:15 reporting multiple same-day absences; no platform or routing event was recorded.
Independent recalculation matched every reported service-level interval exactly, with a maximum difference of 0.0 percentage points; therefore, no actual mismatch was found.

primary_root_cause_detail: Same-day absences beginning at 09:15 caused a center-wide decline in logged-in and productive staffing while scheduled headcount remained unchanged. Productive staffing fell below forecast-required capacity, driving high occupancy, longer waits, and sustained service-level degradation.
recommended_actions: Activate same-day absence contingencies, including reserve staffing, voluntary overtime, and cross-skilled backup agents.
Create real-time alerts when logged-in staffing falls materially below schedule or forecast-required capacity.
Prioritize staffing recovery for the lowest-performing queues while preserving balanced coverage across all queues.
Review absence-notification and escalation procedures so workforce management can intervene before the capacity gap expands.
Monitor service level, ASA, occupancy, and backlog after staffing restoration to confirm recovery.

rejected_hypotheses.reason: Post-incident demand was only 6.0% above the pre-incident mean and averaged 2.1% below forecast, insufficient to explain the severity of the degradation.
Post-incident mean AHT decreased 0.3% and was approximately in line with forecast.
Mean adherence increased from 92.2% to 93.7%; the loss occurred in logged-in headcount, not adherence among available agents.
No agents were recorded in training during any interval.
No routing event was recorded, and staffing and service-level deterioration occurred across every visible queue.
No platform event was visible, and the timing aligns directly with the workforce absence notice and measured staffing loss.
Reported service level matched the specified count-based recalculation in all 16 intervals.
Actual post-incident offered volume and AHT were broadly at or below forecast; the material variance was actual productive staffing falling beneath required capacity.

stakeholder_summary: CC-002 was caused by a confirmed center-wide staffing shortfall. Multiple same-day absences began at 09:15, reducing productive staffing by 25.6% while scheduled headcount stayed at 49. Demand rose moderately but remained below forecast overall, and AHT, adherence, routing, platform, training, and metric-quality explanations were not supported.
